questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.explanation: CA-125: marker for serous epithelial ovarian Ca. Also elevated in endometriosis, PID, menstruation (non-specific). Used for monitoring, not screening.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.explanation: Asherman's syndrome: intrauterine adhesions (synechiae) after D&C/infection → amenorrhea, infertility. Diagnosis: hysteroscopy. Treatment: hysteroscopic adhesiolysis + estrogen.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.explanation: Ectopic pregnancy: 95% in fallopian tube. Most common site: AMPULLA (70%). Then isthmus (12%). Cornual/interstitial: most dangerous (ruptures late, more hemorrhage).

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.question_text: FIGO staging of cervical cancer: stage IIB?
questions.explanation: FIGO cervical Ca: I=cervix only, IIA=upper vagina no parametrium, IIB=parametrial involvement, IIIA=lower 1/3 vagina, IIIB=pelvic wall/hydronephrosis, IVA=bladder/rectum, IVB=distant mets.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.question_text: Most common ovarian tumor in young women?
questions.explanation: Dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma): most common benign ovarian tumor in reproductive age. Contains ectodermal elements (hair, teeth, sebum). Rokitansky protuberance.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.question_text: A 26-year-old nulliparous female presents with chronic, severe pelvic pain that worsens significantly during menstruation (dysmenorrhea) and intercourse (dyspareunia). She has been trying to conceive for 2 years without success. Pelvic examination reveals a fixed, retroverted uterus and tender nodules along the uterosacral ligaments. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an adnexal mass with diffuse, low-level internal echoes ('ground glass appearance'). What is the definitive method of diagnosis?

options.B: Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy of lesions

questions.explanation: This clinical presentation is highly indicative of Endometriosis, with the ultrasound showcasing an endometrioma ('chocolate cyst'). While imaging and symptoms point to the diagnosis, visualization and histological confirmation via laparoscopy remain the diagnostic gold standard.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.question_text: A 53-year-old postmenopausal female presents with a 2-week history of painless vaginal bleeding. She has a history of type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 34 kg/m²). She has never been pregnant. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial stripe measuring 11 mm. What is the most appropriate next step in the clinical evaluation of this patient?

options.A: Reassure the patient and repeat the ultrasound in 6 months
options.B: Initiate continuous combination hormone replacement therapy
options.D: Schedule an immediate total laparoscopic hysterectomy

questions.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) is the classic presentation of endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Risk factors include obesity, diabetes, and nulliparity due to unopposed estrogen. An endometrial thickness >4 mm in a postmenopausal woman warrants tissue sampling via endometrial biopsy or D&C to rule out hyperplasia or malignancy.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.question_text: A 31-year-old female presents to her gynecologist due to an abnormal screening Pap smear showing High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL). What is the next mandatory step in management?

options.A: Repeat the Pap smear in 6 months
options.B: Perform a reflex HPV DNA test

questions.explanation: An HSIL Pap smear result carries a high risk of underlying cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 2/3) or invasive cervical carcinoma. Immediate evaluation via colposcopy with endocervical sampling/directed biopsies is required. Reflex HPV testing is not indicated for high-grade cytology as management will not change based on the status.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old postmenopausal female presents with an adnexal mass. Surgical staging confirms a stage IA granulosa cell tumor of the ovary. Histopathological evaluation reveals sheets of cells organized around small fluid-filled cavities containing eosinophilic debris, resembling immature follicles. What are these diagnostic structures called, and what serum marker is utilized to monitor for recurrence?
questions.explanation: Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord-stromal malignancies that secrete estrogen. Microscopic evaluation classically demonstrates Call-Exner bodies (microfollicular spaces containing eosinophilic fluid). Inhibin B is highly sensitive and specific for these tumors, making it the ideal biomarker for tracking disease recurrence.

questions.subject: OBGYN
questions.question_text: A 16-year-old adolescent female presents with primary amenorrhea. Physical examination reveals normal breast development but completely absent axillary and pubic hair. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a short, blind-ending vaginal pouch and an completely absent uterus and fallopian tubes. Karyotype analysis confirms a 46,XY chromosomal profile. What is the most definitive underlying pathophysiology?

options.B: A mutation in the gene encoding the androgen receptor causing complete tissue insensitivity
options.C: Agenesis of the Mullerian ducts (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome)
options.D: Inability of the fetal testes to produce anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH)

questions.explanation: This patient presents with Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS). Testes develop normally in utero and secrete testosterone and AMH. AMH causes regression of the Mullerian ducts, so no uterus or upper vagina forms. Due to completely non-functional androgen receptors, peripheral tissues respond to converted estrogen, resulting in female secondary traits (breasts) but no androgen-dependent hair growth (axillary/pubic).
